An auxiliary is something — a person, a group, a device, or a word — whose entire purpose is to support, assist, or back up something else that is the main or primary thing. It is never the star of the show. It exists in service of another.

Think of it this way: if the main thing is a king, the auxiliary is the loyal advisor standing just behind him — essential, but not the king.
The Key Characteristics of an Auxiliary

To call something an auxiliary, it typically has these qualities:

1. It is secondary, not primary.
It is not the main thing. There is always a "main" that comes first, and the auxiliary plays a supporting role around it.

2. It provides support that the main thing needs.
It fills a gap, adds capability, or handles tasks the main thing cannot or should not do alone.

3. It is often a backup or reserve.
Many auxiliaries exist specifically for situations where the main thing is overwhelmed, unavailable, or needs help.
The Different Contexts Where "Auxiliary" Is Used as a Noun

The word shows up in several fields, but the same core idea runs through all of them.

1. In Grammar — The Auxiliary Verb

This is probably the most important use of the word for everyday learners.

In grammar, an auxiliary (also called a helping verb) is a verb that works alongside the main verb in a sentence to help express things like tense (when something happens), possibility, obligation, or whether something is passive or active.

The auxiliaries in English include words like:
is, are, was, were, have, has, had, do, does, did, will, would, shall, should, can, could, may, might, must

Look at these examples:

"She is running."

Here, running is the main verb — the real action. But is is the auxiliary. Alone, "She running" is incomplete and broken. The auxiliary is supports the main verb and makes the whole thing grammatically correct and meaningful.

"He should study."

Here, study is the main action. But should is the auxiliary — it adds the meaning of advice or obligation. Without it, you just get "He study," which is wrong.

"The letter was written by Maria."

Here, written is the main verb. Was is the auxiliary that creates the passive voice (the subject receives the action rather than doing it).

Key insight: An auxiliary verb cannot usually stand alone as the main action of a sentence. It needs a main verb to work with. Its job is to assist, not to lead.

Some auxiliaries can also double as main verbs, depending on context:

  • "She is a doctor." → Here, is is the main verb (no other verb present).
  • "She is working." → Here, is is the auxiliary, supporting working.

2. In the Military — Auxiliary Troops or Forces

In military language, an auxiliary refers to a force of soldiers that is not part of the core, regular army but is brought in or organised to support and assist it.

Historically, these were often foreign soldiers, local recruits, or volunteers who fought alongside a nation's main army. They handled tasks like guarding territory, supplying the front lines, or reinforcing weakened positions.

The regular army is the main force. The auxiliaries exist to help it succeed.

Example: "Rome relied heavily on its auxiliaries to hold the borders of the empire."

3. In Organisations — An Auxiliary Group

An auxiliary can also be a group of people — often volunteers — who are attached to a larger organisation and provide support to it.

Example: "She volunteered with the hospital auxiliary."

This means she was part of a volunteer group that supports the hospital — perhaps by fundraising, staffing reception desks, or delivering food to patients. The auxiliary is not the hospital itself; it exists to assist the hospital in doing its work.

Other examples: a police auxiliary (civilians who assist the police), a veterans' auxiliary (family members or supporters who help a veterans' organisation).

4. In Technology and Engineering — A Backup or Secondary System

In technical contexts, an auxiliary is a secondary system or device that supports or backs up the primary one.

Example: "The ship switched to its auxiliary when the main engine failed."

Here, the auxiliary (short for auxiliary engine or auxiliary power system) is a backup power source. It is not used during normal operation — it exists for emergencies or supplementary needs.

You'll often see this in aviation (auxiliary power units on planes), ships, generators, and industrial machinery.

No matter the context, if you see the word auxiliary used as a noun, always think: "This is the helper, not the hero."

ContextThe "Main" ThingThe Auxiliary
  • In grammar → The main verb does the action. The auxiliary helps it express time, possibility, or mood.
  • In the military → The regular army is the main force. The auxiliaries support it.
  • In organisations → The main institution (hospital, police, etc.) is primary. The auxiliary group supports it.
  • In engineering → The main system runs things normally. The auxiliary backs it up or supplements it.
One Sentence to Remember It Forever
An auxiliary is a helper or supporter that exists to assist something more primary than itself — never the main act, always the essential backup.

"The verb 'will' is an auxiliary in the sentence 'She will arrive tomorrow.'"
→ Will supports the main verb arrive. It tells you about future time. It is the helper.

"The Red Cross auxiliary raised funds for the local chapter."
→ A volunteer support group helped the main Red Cross chapter do its work.

"The generator served as an auxiliary during the blackout."
→ The generator was the backup system, stepping in when the main power supply failed.

In every case, the auxiliary is indispensable — but it always knows its role: to serve, support, and strengthen the thing it stands behind.
